title: 3-D Objects: Views, Plans, Elevations and Nets
seo_title: Grade 9 3-D Objects Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Revise properties and definitions of the 5 Platonic solids; recognise and describe the properties of spheres and cylinders; use nets to create models of geometric solids; draw and interpret views of 3-D objects from different positions.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 9 3-D objects worksheets: plans, front and side elevations, nets and faces, edges and vertices. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Plan: from above. Elevation: from the front or side.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A plan is the view from above. An elevation is the view from the front or the side.
  • Draw only what you can see from that direction.
  • A net is a flat pattern that folds into the solid.
  • Euler: F + V − E = 2 for polyhedra.

Examples

Example

A row of stacks 2, 3, 1

front elevation shows heights 2, 3, 1

Answer: plan: 3 squares in a row

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
What you knowDraw what you see.
Plan or elevation?The plan is from above.
Overlapping netEach face needs its own place.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 6 rectangles in 3 matching pairs fold into a rectangular prism. Opposite faces are the same size.

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 2 triangles (the bases) and 3 rectangles fold into a triangular prism. The bases are right triangles here; a prism’s bases do not have to be equilateral.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 1 square base and 4 triangles that meet at one point fold into a square-based pyramid.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 4 triangles fold into a triangular pyramid: one is the base and the other 3 meet at a point.

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 2 pentagons (the bases) and 5 rectangles fold into a pentagonal prism.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 1 hexagon base and 6 triangles that meet at one point fold into a hexagonal pyramid. A pyramid is named after its base.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 1 rectangle base and 4 triangles that meet at one point fold into a rectangular pyramid. The base is a rectangle that is not a square, so the triangles on the long sides and short sides differ.

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 1 pentagon base and 5 triangles that meet at one point fold into a pentagonal pyramid.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 2 hexagons (the bases) and 6 rectangles fold into a hexagonal prism.

items.q: Which net folds into a pentagonal prism?
items.e: A has 2 pentagons on opposite edges of a strip of 5 rectangles. One wrong net is a pentagonal pyramid, one has only 4 rectangles (it cannot close), and one has both pentagons on the same edge, so they fold onto the same end.

items.q: Which net folds into a closed cylinder?
items.e: A is right: the rectangle is as long as the distance around each circle. In one wrong net the rectangle is only as long as the diameter, so it is far too short to wrap around the circles. The others are a triangular prism and a net with only 1 circle.

items.q: Which part of a cylinder’s net becomes the curved surface?
items.e: The rectangle rolls up into a tube. The 2 circles are the flat top and bottom.

items.q: In the net of a cylinder, the length of the rectangle that touches the circles is equal to …
items.e: That edge wraps once around each circle, so it is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r.

items.q: This is the net of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. How long is the rectangle? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3,14 × 3 = 18,84 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 12 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3,14 × 5 = 31,4 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: This is the net of a cylinder with radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. How long is the rectangle? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3,14 × 4 = 25,12 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 6 cm and a height of 15 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3,14 × 6 = 37,68 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 9 cm and a height of 20 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3,14 × 9 = 56,52 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A can has a diameter of 10 cm. Its paper label wraps around the can once with no overlap. How long is the label? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d = 3,14 × 10 = 31,4 cm. 2 × π × d uses the diameter as if it were the radius.

items.q: A can has a diameter of 12 cm. Its paper label wraps around the can once with no overlap. How long is the label? (Use π ≈ 3,14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d = 3,14 × 12 = 37,68 cm. 2 × π × d uses the diameter as if it were the radius.

items.q: This is a triangular prism. How many faces does it have?
items.e: A triangular prism has 5 faces (2 triangles + 3 rectangles), 9 edges (3 + 3 + 3) and 6 vertices (3 + 3). You can see only 3 faces, but the bottom and the back end count too.

items.q: This is a triangular prism. How many edges does it have?
items.e: A triangular prism has 5 faces (2 triangles + 3 rectangles), 9 edges (3 + 3 + 3) and 6 vertices (3 + 3). 3 edges round each end and 3 joining the ends.

items.q: How many vertices does a triangular prism have?
items.e: A triangular prism has 5 faces (2 triangles + 3 rectangles), 9 edges (3 + 3 + 3) and 6 vertices (3 + 3).

items.q: This is a rectangular prism. How many edges does it have?
items.e: A rectangular prism has 6 faces (2 rectangles + 4 rectangles), 12 edges (4 + 4 + 4) and 8 vertices (4 + 4). Dashed lines show edges at the back that you cannot see.

items.q: This is a pentagonal prism. How many faces does it have?
items.e: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces (2 pentagons + 5 rectangles), 15 edges (5 + 5 + 5) and 10 vertices (5 + 5). Dashed lines show edges at the back that you cannot see.

items.q: How many edges does a pentagonal prism have?
items.e: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces (2 pentagons + 5 rectangles), 15 edges (5 + 5 + 5) and 10 vertices (5 + 5). Do not forget the 5 edges that join the two ends.

items.q: This is a pentagonal prism. How many vertices does it have?
items.e: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces (2 pentagons + 5 rectangles), 15 edges (5 + 5 + 5) and 10 vertices (5 + 5).

items.q: This is a hexagonal prism. How many faces does it have?
items.e: A hexagonal prism has 8 faces (2 hexagons + 6 rectangles), 18 edges (6 + 6 + 6) and 12 vertices (6 + 6). Do not forget the 2 hexagon ends.

items.q: How many edges does a hexagonal prism have?
items.e: A hexagonal prism has 8 faces (2 hexagons + 6 rectangles), 18 edges (6 + 6 + 6) and 12 vertices (6 + 6). Edges round both ends (6 + 6) plus 6 joining them.

items.q: This is a hexagonal prism. How many vertices does it have?
items.e: A hexagonal prism has 8 faces (2 hexagons + 6 rectangles), 18 edges (6 + 6 + 6) and 12 vertices (6 + 6).

items.q: How many faces does an octagonal prism have?
items.e: An octagonal prism has 10 faces (2 octagons + 8 rectangles), 24 edges (8 + 8 + 8) and 16 vertices (8 + 8).

items.q: How many edges does an octagonal prism have?
items.e: An octagonal prism has 10 faces (2 octagons + 8 rectangles), 24 edges (8 + 8 + 8) and 16 vertices (8 + 8).

items.q: How many vertices does a heptagonal prism have?
items.e: A heptagonal prism has 9 faces (2 heptagons + 7 rectangles), 21 edges (7 + 7 + 7) and 14 vertices (7 + 7).

items.q: A prism has 8 faces. What shape is its cross-section?
items.e: Faces = 2 ends + the number of sides. 8 − 2 = 6 sides, so the ends are hexagons. (Heptagon uses the pyramid rule: 8 − 1.)

items.q: A prism has 18 edges. What shape is its cross-section?
items.e: A prism has 3 edges for every side of its end (round the front, round the back, and joining them). 18 ÷ 3 = 6, so the ends are hexagons.

items.q: A prism has 10 vertices. What is its name?
items.e: Half the vertices are on each end: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so the ends are pentagons.

items.q: How many more vertices does a hexagonal prism have than a hexagonal pyramid?
items.e: Prism: 6 + 6 = 12 vertices. Pyramid: 6 on the base + 1 apex = 7. 12 − 7 = 5.

items.q: Which has more edges, a pentagonal prism or a pentagonal pyramid, and by how many?
items.e: Prism: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 edges. Pyramid: 5 round the base + 5 up to the apex = 10. 15 − 10 = 5.

items.q: A prism’s cross-section has n sides. Which rule gives its number of faces?
items.e: There are n rectangles plus the 2 ends: n + 2. (n + 1 is the rule for a pyramid, 2 × n gives the vertices and 3 × n gives the edges.)

items.q: A triangular prism and a square-based pyramid both have 5 faces. How else are they different?
c: They have the same number of edges
The prism has 5 vertices and the pyramid has 6
The prism has 6 vertices and the pyramid has 5
items.e: Triangular prism: 9 edges, 6 vertices. Square-based pyramid: 8 edges, 5 vertices.
